base:
  image: ubuntu:24.04
  config: rwx/base 1.2.0

tasks:
  - key: code
    call: git/clone 2.2.0
    with:
      repository: https://github.com/elviskahoro/buridan-ui.git
      ref: ${{ init.commit-sha }}

  # Checksum-pinned uv installer: fails closed if the script at the versioned
  # URL ever changes. No packaged uv/install leaf exists in the RWX catalog.
  - key: uv-install
    run: |
      set -euo pipefail
      script="$(mktemp)"
      trap 'rm -f "${script}"' EXIT
      curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/0.11.29/install.sh -o "${script}"
      echo "504a79fd2ed0dcd47e7f04f0792cfd0871f62e24a7fe40fa8ae0f563a369f2bd  ${script}" | sha256sum -c -
      sh "${script}"
      echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$RWX_ENV/PATH"

  # --- Dagger toolchain (Layer A): no `use: code`, so these cache across commits.
  - key: dagger-cli-install
    run: |
      set -euo pipefail
      curl -fsSLO https://dl.dagger.io/dagger/releases/0.21.8/dagger_v0.21.8_linux_amd64.tar.gz
      echo "53e226c7da8fb75171e58c35759d736d961ce8b3a12db0baa7b7107954fccc5a  dagger_v0.21.8_linux_amd64.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c -
      mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
      tar -xzf dagger_v0.21.8_linux_amd64.tar.gz -C "$HOME/.local/bin" dagger
      echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$RWX_ENV/PATH"

  # Locked Dagger SDK venv, filtered to ci/ lock inputs only.
  - key: dagger-sdk-install
    use: [uv-install, code]
    filter:
      - ci/pyproject.toml
      - ci/uv.lock
    run: |
      uv sync --frozen --project ci
      echo "$PWD/ci/.venv/bin" >> "$RWX_ENV/PATH"

  - key: dagger-engine-warm
    use: [dagger-cli-install]
    docker: preserve-data
    run: |
      set -euo pipefail
      for i in 1 2 3; do docker pull registry.dagger.io/engine:v0.21.8 && exit 0; sleep 5; done
      exit 1

  # Captain (rwx/install-captain) wraps pytest for flaky-test retries and
  # results in the RWX UI. RWX supplies its access token automatically.
  - key: captain
    call: rwx/install-captain 1.2.0

  # Trunk analytics uploader, checksum-pinned like the other installers.
  - key: trunk-analytics-install
    run: |
      set -euo pipefail
      curl -fsSLO https://github.com/trunk-io/analytics-cli/releases/download/0.16.3/trunk-analytics-cli-x86_64-unknown-linux.tar.gz
      echo "1ea62c660a5ec271746aad93b8109bd41645fab9a72043ec70ea94f4883c04c4  trunk-analytics-cli-x86_64-unknown-linux.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c -
      mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
      tar -xzf trunk-analytics-cli-x86_64-unknown-linux.tar.gz -C "$HOME/.local/bin" trunk-analytics-cli
      echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$RWX_ENV/PATH"

  - key: pytest
    use: [code, dagger-cli-install, dagger-sdk-install, dagger-engine-warm, captain]
    docker: true
    timeout: 30m
    # Uncached so the required status is never a replayed verdict (a same-head
    # re-trigger once went green in ~530ms); upstream install caches stay.
    cache: false
    # The Dagger program (ci/main.py) runs pytest in a container with node
    # present (pinned there) and pytest-reportlog pinned via --with; it exports
    # tmp/ (log.json + junit) to ci-out/. Captain parses the report log. The
    # retry writes its own JUnit file so the original failure is preserved.
    run: |
      export CI_OUT_DIR="$PWD/tmp"
      captain run buridan-ui-pytest \
        --command "dagger run python ci/main.py test" \
        --retry-command "dagger run python ci/main.py test --junit-name retry.xml -- {{ tests }}" \
        --retries 1 \
        --test-results "tmp/log.json" \
        --print-summary
    outputs:
      artifacts:
        - key: junit
          path: tmp/junit

  # Trunk Flaky Tests upload. Separate from `pytest`, and `RWX: tests` is bound
  # to the pytest task alone, so this task can never red the required check —
  # not on a Trunk outage, not on a vault miss. Runs after pytest finishes
  # (pass or fail). `upload-trunk` is only "true" on the push legs the vault
  # grant covers (main and the merge-queue branches): on any other ref RWX
  # fails vault-secret resolution before the script's empty-token guard can
  # fire, and a skipped task is green for the run. The author gate stays
  # alongside — vault grants match repo + ref, never author, and the repo is
  # public, so non-owner PR legs (forks, Dependabot, bots) must not see the
  # token even if the grant is widened. TRUNK_API_TOKEN lives in the
  # `buridan-ui-trunk-flaky` vault (Flaky Tests token only); cache: false +
  # cache-key: excluded keep it out of the cache fingerprint.
  - key: trunk-upload
    after: ${{ pytest.finished }}
    use: [code, trunk-analytics-install]
    if: ${{ init.pr-author == 'elviskahoro' && init.upload-trunk == 'true' }}
    cache: false
    env:
      TRUNK_API_TOKEN:
        value: ${{ vaults.buridan-ui-trunk-flaky.secrets.TRUNK_API_TOKEN }}
        cache-key: excluded
      TRUNK_ORG_URL_SLUG: sanhedrin
      JUNIT_DIR: ${{ tasks.pytest.artifacts.junit }}
      HEAD_SHA: ${{ init.commit-sha }}
      HEAD_BRANCH: ${{ init.branch }}
      PR_NUMBER: ${{ init.pr-number }}
      HEAD_AUTHOR: ${{ init.pr-author }}
    run: |
      set -euo pipefail
      if [ -z "${TRUNK_API_TOKEN}" ]; then
        echo "warning: TRUNK_API_TOKEN is unavailable; skipping upload"
        exit 0
      fi
      # The clone's .git is stripped (code.cleanup-git-dir), so pass the git
      # metadata explicitly instead of letting the uploader read it.
      args=(
        --junit-paths "${JUNIT_DIR}/*.xml"
        --use-uncloned-repo
        --repo-url https://github.com/elviskahoro/buridan-ui.git
        --repo-head-sha "${HEAD_SHA}"
        --repo-head-branch "${HEAD_BRANCH:-unknown}"
        --repo-head-author-name "${HEAD_AUTHOR}"
        --repo-head-commit-epoch "$(date +%s)"
      )
      if [ -n "${PR_NUMBER}" ]; then
        args+=(--pr-number "${PR_NUMBER}")
      fi
      trunk-analytics-cli upload "${args[@]}"

# Plan: RWX PR preview app for buridan-ui

## Context
reflex-starter-template has `.rwx/preview.yml` that builds the Reflex frontend export, then serves it plus the Reflex backend behind Caddy as an RWX `app:` at `pr-<N>`. buridan-ui has no preview/Caddyfile yet. Port it.

## Changes
1. `.rwx/preview.yml` — copy of the reference, adapted:
   - repository -> `https://github.com/elviskahoro/buridan-ui.git`
   - keep `uv` 0.11.29 + sha from `.rwx/tests.yml`, `git/clone 2.2.0` as in tests.yml (repo convention); drop `preserve-git-dir`/full-depth unless `reflex export` needs git (not expected)
   - tasks: code -> uv-install -> deps (`uv sync --frozen`) -> bun-install (pinned bun-v1.4.3, checksum as in reference) -> reflex-export -> system-deps (caddy, unzip) -> build (unzip to /srv, rewrite `localhost:8000` env asset to `location.origin`) -> preview (`app:` endpoint `pr-${{ init.pull-request-number }}`, port 3000) -> share-link
   - triggers: `pull_request` (status check name `preview`, base ref main only, matching tests.yml `if`), `cli`.
2. `Caddyfile` at repo root — copy of reference (`:{$PORT}`, `/ping`, proxy `/_event/*`, `/_upload*` to :8000, static from /srv with 404 fallback).
3. Docs: short "PR previews" note in `CONTRIBUTING.md` (commands: `rwx lint`, `rwx run .rwx/preview.yml --init pull-request-number=0 --wait`, `rwx apps share pr-0`).

## Open points to verify while implementing
- buridan-ui's frontend env file may differ from the reference (`grep -rl localhost:8000 /srv/assets`); confirm the rewrite hits the right file and generated var shape matches reflex 0.10.0 export.
- Whether `reflex export` needs extra setup (generated assets via `scripts/`, tailwind plugins via bun) — check the run.
- Backend startup needs `reflex.lock`/env vars? Check `app` imports at `reflex run --backend-only`.

## Verification
- `rwx lint .rwx/preview.yml`
- `rwx run .rwx/preview.yml --init pull-request-number=0 --wait` (use `--access-token "$RWX_ACCESS_TOKEN_*"` if needed); check `share-link` log, `rwx apps share pr-0`, curl `/` = 200 and `/ping` = pong.
- Not verified locally: WebSocket event round trip (same caveat as reference).

 - Fast mode for Claude Code gives faster output on this session's model if it supports fast mode, and otherwise switches the session to Claude Opus. It can be toggled with /fast.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ExitPlanMode
tools.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

tool.description: The tool this prompt applies to

prompt.description: Semantic description of the action, e.g. "run tests", "install dependencies"

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__conductor__AskUserQuestion

question.description: The question to ask the user

options.description: Up to 4 options for the user to choose from. Do not include 'Other' - it is automatically provided.

header.description: Short label displayed above the question.

multiSelect.description: If true, user can select multiple options. Answers are comma-separated.

# Plan: RWX PR preview app for buridan-ui

## Context
reflex-starter-template has `.rwx/preview.yml` that builds the Reflex frontend export, then serves it plus the Reflex backend behind Caddy as an RWX `app:` at `pr-<N>`. buridan-ui has no preview/Caddyfile yet. Port it.

## Changes
1. `.rwx/preview.yml` — copy of the reference, adapted:
   - repository -> `https://github.com/elviskahoro/buridan-ui.git`
   - keep `uv` 0.11.29 + sha from `.rwx/tests.yml`, `git/clone 2.2.0` as in tests.yml (repo convention); drop `preserve-git-dir`/full-depth unless `reflex export` needs git (not expected)
   - tasks: code -> uv-install -> deps (`uv sync --frozen`) -> bun-install (pinned bun-v1.4.3, checksum as in reference) -> reflex-export -> system-deps (caddy, unzip) -> build (unzip to /srv, rewrite `localhost:8000` env asset to `location.origin`) -> preview (`app:` endpoint `pr-${{ init.pull-request-number }}`, port 3000) -> share-link
   - triggers: `pull_request` (status check name `preview`, base ref main only, matching tests.yml `if`), `cli`.
2. `Caddyfile` at repo root — copy of reference (`:{$PORT}`, `/ping`, proxy `/_event/*`, `/_upload*` to :8000, static from /srv with 404 fallback).
3. Docs: short "PR previews" note in `CONTRIBUTING.md` (commands: `rwx lint`, `rwx run .rwx/preview.yml --init pull-request-number=0 --wait`, `rwx apps share pr-0`).

## Open points to verify while implementing
- buridan-ui's frontend env file may differ from the reference (`grep -rl localhost:8000 /srv/assets`); confirm the rewrite hits the right file and generated var shape matches reflex 0.10.0 export.
- Whether `reflex export` needs extra setup (generated assets via `scripts/`, tailwind plugins via bun) — check the run.
- Backend startup needs `reflex.lock`/env vars? Check `app` imports at `reflex run --backend-only`.

## Verification
- `rwx lint .rwx/preview.yml`
- `rwx run .rwx/preview.yml --init pull-request-number=0 --wait` (use `--access-token "$RWX_ACCESS_TOKEN_*"` if needed); check `share-link` log, `rwx apps share pr-0`, curl `/` = 200 and `/ping` = pong.

- **`.rwx/preview.yml`**: ported from the reflex-starter pipeline. It triggers on PRs to `main` (status check `preview`) and from the CLI. The app is served at `pr-<N>` on port 3000. It uses this repo's pinned uv 0.11.29 and `git/clone 2.2.0`.
- **`Caddyfile`**: copied unchanged from the reference. It serves the static export and proxies `/_event` and `/_upload` to the backend.
- **One change beyond a straight port**: the `deps` task filter now includes `cli`, `app` and `components`. Without them `uv sync` fails because the root package needs `cli/README.md`.
- **Not verified**: a WebSocket event round trip. The `build` task rewrites the baked-in `localhost:8000` URL to the page origin, and that rewrite is undocumented by RWX and Reflex.
- **Lint**: `rwx lint` only warns that `git/clone 2.2.0` is outdated (2.4.1 is current). I kept 2.2.0 to match `tests.yml`.

The run needed `--access-token "$RWX_ACCESS_TOKEN_ELVISKAHORO"`.

13	- Use `gh pr create --base main` to create a PR onto the target branch. Keep the title under 80 characters. Keep the description under five sentences, unless the user instructed you otherwise. Describe not just changes made in this session but ALL changes in the workspace diff.
14

16	
17	## PR Description Template
18	
19	This workspace has a PR template, which is provided below. Use it for writing the PR description, filling it in based on the changes made.
20	
21	```markdown
22	<!-- markdownlint-disable MD041 -->
23	<!-- Full conventions: `create_pr` prompt in .conductor/settings.toml. Title: sentence case, why-focused, no Conventional Commits prefix, no ticket ID. Never summarize the diff. Drop empty sections. -->
24	
25	## Why
26	
27	## Trade-offs
28	
29	## Risks
30	
31	## Test plan
32	
33	## Links
34	
35	```
36	
37	## Organization prompt
38	
39	Below are the organization's preferences. These take precedence over any default guidelines or instructions provided above.
40	
41	<!-- Canonical source: flox-conductor-sandbox prompts/conductor/create-pr.md.
42	     Installed into a repo's .conductor settings [prompts].create_pr by
43	     scripts/install-conductor-prompts.py — do not hand-edit the TOML copy.
44	     Upstream history: gtm-sdk prompts/conductor/create-pr.md (incl. #921).
45	     Repo-specific references (Linear, design/ artifacts,
46	     roborev) follow the cross-repo conventions — where a repo's own
47	     instructions differ, the repo wins. -->
48	
49	# Creating Pull Requests
50	
51	## The principle: why over what
52	
53	A PR description's job is to give the reviewer what the diff *can't*: motivation, alternatives considered, risks worth scrutinizing, and a trail back to the originating context. The diff itself is the source of truth for what changed — paraphrasing it in the description is duplicate work that rots the moment someone force-pushes.
54	
55	Concretely:
56	
57	- Lead with the **problem**, not the change.
58	- Name the **alternatives** you considered, briefly. Skip if there were no meaningful ones.
59	- Call out what reviewers should **scrutinize**, not what they should take on faith.
60	- Link the **breadcrumb trail** — Linear ticket, design spec/plan, predecessor PR.
61	- **Never** summarize the diff. The reviewer is about to read it.
62	
63	A reader who skims your description should walk away with the mental model needed to read the diff with intention.
64	
65	## Workflow
66	
67	### Step 1: Pre-flight checks
68	
69	Before drafting, run these in a single batch of parallel `Bash` calls:
70	
71	```bash
72	git status                                          # working tree clean?
73	git branch --show-current                           # current branch?
74	git rev-parse --abbrev-ref @{upstream} 2>/dev/null  # is there a remote tracking ref?
75	git log @{upstream}..HEAD --oneline 2>/dev/null     # any unpushed commits?
76	git log main..HEAD --oneline                        # commits beyond main?
77	git diff main...HEAD --stat                         # surface area?
78	gh pr view --json url,state 2>/dev/null             # does a PR already exist?
79	gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef --jq .defaultBranchRef.name  # confirm base
80	```
81	
82	Stop and surface the problem to the user if any of these is true:
83	
84	- The working tree has uncommitted changes — ask the user whether to commit, stash, or abandon.
85	- The branch has no upstream / is not pushed — confirm with the user before pushing.
86	- The branch has zero commits beyond the base — there's nothing to PR.
87	- A PR already exists for this branch — use `gh pr edit` to update it, not `gh pr create`.
88	
89	Don't paper over these by force-pushing, amending, or running `git push -f`. The repo's agent instructions (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) apply: destructive operations need explicit user approval.
90	
91	### Step 2: Gather context for the "Why"
92	
93	A strong Why section comes from upstream artifacts, not from the diff. Pull from these sources in parallel where possible:
94	
95	**Linear ticket** — if the branch name matches `(feature|agent)/<team>-<number>-<slug>` (e.g., `feature/ai-268-foo`, `agent/eng-1234-bar`):
96	
97	1. Extract the ticket ID with a regex like `[A-Z]+-\d+` (case-insensitive).
98	2. Read it via `mcp__linear__get_issue` with the identifier.
99	3. Lift the problem statement and acceptance criteria into the Why section — **paraphrase, don't paste**. A wall of quoted ticket text isn't a PR description.
100	4. Save the URL for the Links section.
101	
102	Skip the Linear lookup when the repo doesn't use Linear (no Linear MCP configured, no matching branch pattern) — rely on the sources below.
103	
104	**GitHub issue** — if the user linked or named a GitHub issue this session (a URL, `#NNN`, or an issue the branch was created for, e.g., `conductor/gtm-sdk-issue-608`):
105	
106	1. Note whether it's same-repo or cross-repo (a bare `#NNN` or number is same-repo; a URL or `owner/repo#NNN` names the repo explicitly — keep that `owner/repo` around for every later step). Fetch it with `gh issue view <number>` for a same-repo issue, or `gh issue view <number> --repo <owner/repo>` otherwise, to confirm it's still open and pull the problem statement into the Why section — paraphrase, don't paste.
107	2. Ask yourself (and, if unclear, the user) whether this PR **fully** resolves the issue or only partial work. Carry that determination into Step 7's Links section and Step 9.
108	3. Save the issue reference for the Links section either way.
109	
110	**Design artifacts** — scan `design/` (when the repo uses the design-artifact convention) for backlog/done files matching the branch topic:
111	
112	```bash
113	ls "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/design/" 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "<topic-keyword>"
114	```
115	
116	- `*-spec-*.md` files carry motivation, constraints, trade-offs.
117	- `*-plan-*.md` files carry scope (and by elision, what's out of scope).
118	- Read the matching artifact in full before drafting.
119	
120	**Git history**:
121	
122	- `git log main..HEAD --format='%s%n%b%n---'` — commit subjects and bodies often capture in-flight decisions better than the final diff.
123	
124	**Current conversation**:
125	
126	- If the user discussed alternatives, made decisions mid-flight, or set constraints earlier in this session, those belong in Trade-offs or Risks.
127	
128	If none of these sources establishes a clear Why, **stop and ask the user**. Don't fabricate motivation — a confident-sounding-but-vague Why is worse than asking.
129	
130	### Step 3: Commit local changes
131	
132	If the pre-flight check surfaced uncommitted changes that belong in this PR, commit them **before** running roborev — roborev reviews committed history, not the working tree, so uncommitted edits would be invisible to it.
133	
134	- Stage only the files that belong in this PR. Skip tool-local cruft (e.g., `.agents/`, `.claude/`, Conductor-local files) unless the user explicitly opts in.
135	- Commit without asking for approval: run `git commit` directly once the files are staged. The commit message should mirror the PR title's intent (sentence-cased, why-focused) — not a Conventional Commits subject. The Step 8 draft approval is still the only user-approval gate before push.
136	- Do **not** push yet. Push happens in Step 11, after squash, roborev, the user-confirmation gate, and the rebase.
137	
138	If the working tree is already clean, skip this step.
139	
140	### Step 4: Squash to a coherent set of commits
141	
142	**Hard gate: squash before roborev, roborev before the user-confirmation gate, confirmation before push.** All three must happen before the branch hits `origin` so the review (and the merge) operate on the final history, not a noisy timeline.
143	
144	```bash
145	git log main..HEAD --oneline
146	```
147	
148	- **Default to one commit per PR.** Multi-commit PRs are only OK when each commit is independently reviewable and the slices land in order.
149	- Squash with `git rebase -i main` or `git reset --soft main && git commit`. Never use `--no-edit` flags that bypass message review.
150	- The squashed commit message mirrors the PR title's intent (sentence-cased, why-focused) and captures the motivation in the body. No Conventional Commits prefix.
151	- If the branch already has a single commit (or each existing commit is independently reviewable and ordered), skip the rebase but still confirm the count before moving on.
152	- **Never force-push to a shared branch to squash after publication.** Squash *before* the first push.
153	
154	### Step 5: Run relevant tests locally, then roborev review before drafting
155	
156	**Roborev reviews the diff; it does not execute the test suite.** A clean roborev pass says nothing about whether the code runs — it has caught logic/quality issues while a hardcoded assertion in a test file was still broken. Before roborev, run whatever tests cover the changed files:
157	
158	- Identify affected tests by mirroring the changed path under `tests/` (many repos mirror source layout — a change to `pkg/foo.py` often has a matching `tests/.../test_foo.py`) and/or `grep -rn` the changed file's distinctive strings (a literal like an `if:` condition, a flag name) across `tests/` to catch assertions on exact values.
159	- Run the narrowest test target that covers the change (in a uv-based Python repo, `uv run pytest tests/<mirrored-path>`; otherwise the repo's own test command) — full-suite runs are fine too, but don't skip this step because CI will "catch it anyway": local runs take seconds, CI takes minutes.
160	- If a test fails, fix it now and fold the fix into the same commit (Step 3/4), *before* running roborev — don't push and let CI discover it.
161	
162	**Hard gate: do not draft the PR or move toward `git push` until roborev has run and either reported clean or been explicitly acknowledged by the user.** This applies even if the change feels trivial, even if the diff is one line, and even if the user has not asked for review explicitly — the skill always runs roborev before the user is asked to approve a draft.
163	
164	With the squashed commit in place but the branch still local, run a local AI code review with roborev so findings surface *before* the user sees a draft and *before* GitHub sees the diff. Invoke the `roborev` executable directly with the `--wait` flag; Git aliases are optional conveniences and may not exist in cloud sandboxes:
165	
166	```bash
167	roborev review --wait
168	```
169	
170	- `--wait` is **required**, not optional — it blocks until the review completes so findings are available before the draft is shown. Do not run `roborev review` without `--wait`.
171	- A bare `roborev review` — or a leftover post-commit auto-review hook — only **enqueues a background daemon job and returns before a verdict exists**. An enqueue is not a pass: if HEAD already has a queued or running background review, block on it (`roborev review --wait`, or `roborev wait` for the already-enqueued job) so an actual verdict is in hand before drafting. Never report "review enqueued" or a missing verdict as clean.
172	- Capture the outcome (clean, N findings fixed in M rounds, N findings unresolved, unavailable) — Step 8 surfaces it inside the draft preview so the user can see the gate was walked.
173	- **Review loop (no permission prompts):** if roborev surfaces findings, fix them yourself without asking — **every severity counts**, including low and nit. Do not stop, summarize, or ask "fix these?" / "defer or proceed?" because findings are low severity. Fix as many as possible that are small in scope: a wording or error-message change, a missing test case, a missing guard, a rename, a local refactor inside the changed function. Do not fix findings that would reshape the surrounding design, change public interfaces, or touch files outside this PR's scope; for those only, report them to the user with the reason they were not fixed. Put the fixes in a follow-up commit, re-squash (Step 4), and re-run `roborev review --wait` (this step). Repeat until a run comes back clean or only out-of-scope findings remain. Do not ask "fix and rerun?" — that is the default action.
174	- **Loop cap:** stop after 3 fix rounds. If findings remain, or a finding would need a product or design decision rather than a code fix, stop looping and list the unresolved findings in the Step 8 draft preview, so the user decides at the single approval gate. Never amend or force-push past findings silently.
175	- If roborev is unavailable (command not installed, no network), say so explicitly to the user and ask whether to proceed without review. Do not silently skip.
176	- For deeper fix/refine loops, consult the repo's roborev guide skill if it ships one.
177	
178	### Step 6: Draft the title
179	
180	The title is a formal, sentence-cased statement of **why this change exists** — not a conventional commit subject. A reviewer scanning the PR list should understand the *motivation*, not just the area of code touched.
181	
182	Rules:
183	
184	- **Formal, sentence case.** "Eliminate duplicated Attio retry logic across five call sites" — not "attio retry refactor".
185	- **Lead with the why, not the what.** Prefer the problem solved or the outcome enabled over the mechanical change. "Unblock Linear → Attio sync from rate-limit drift" beats "Add retry decorator to Attio client".
186	- **No Conventional Commits prefix.** Do **not** use `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, etc. Even if recent commits or PRs use them, PR titles in this ecosystem are full sentences. Commit messages and PR titles are different surfaces.
187	- **Under 70 characters where possible**, but clarity wins over brevity — GitHub truncates in list views, so front-load the most important words.
188	- **Specific.** "Fix off-by-one in Apollo pagination cursor causing missed contacts" — not "Bug fix" or "Improvements".
189	- **No ticket IDs in the title.** They go in Links.
190	- **No trailing period.**
191	- **Avoid bare imperative verbs** like "Add", "Fix", "Update" as the first word when a why-framing is possible. They're allowed when the why genuinely is the action (e.g., a clear bugfix), but check first whether the motivation can lead instead.
192	
193	Good vs. bad title shapes:
194	
195	| Bad (conventional / what-focused) | Good (formal / why-focused) |
196	| --- | --- |
197	| `feat: add retry decorator` | `Consolidate Attio retry logic to unblock Linear sync` |
198	| `fix: pagination bug` | `Fix off-by-one in Apollo pagination cursor causing missed contacts` |
199	| `refactor: clean up attio client` | `Eliminate divergent retry behavior across Attio call sites` |
200	| `chore: bump deps` | `Bump httpx to 0.27 to pick up the connection-pool leak fix` |
201	
202	### Step 7: Draft the description
203	
204	Use this template. **Drop sections that have nothing meaningful in them** — a section containing "None" or "N/A" is worse than no section.
205	
206	```markdown
207	## Why
208	<1-3 paragraphs. Lead with the problem or constraint. State the motivation. Reference upstream context (ticket, spec) by link, not paraphrase. The reviewer should finish this section understanding what would happen if the PR were *not* merged.>
209	
210	## Trade-offs
211	<Only if there were meaningful alternatives. Format: "Chose X over Y because Z." Skip if the approach was obvious or there was only one reasonable way.>
212	
213	## Risks
214	<What could break that isn't already covered by tests. Note rollback path if non-trivial. Skip for clearly low-risk changes (docs, comments, isolated refactors with full coverage).>
215	
216	## Test plan
217	<Reasoning, not output. "Exercised X path with Y inputs because Z is the highest-risk surface." If full unit coverage exists and the change is small/obvious, skip this section.>
218	
219	## Links
220	- Linear: [TEAM-NNN](https://linear.app/...)
221	- Spec: design/backlog-...-spec-01.md
222	- Plan: design/backlog-...-plan-01.md
223	- Related PRs: #NNN
224	- Closes #NNN (only when Step 2 confirmed this PR fully resolves a same-repo GitHub issue)
225	```
226	
227	Section guidance:
228	
229	| Section | Required? | When to drop it |
230	| --- | --- | --- |
231	| Why | Always | Never. If you can't write a specific one, the work isn't ready. |
232	| Trade-offs | When meaningful alternatives existed | Obvious one-way changes, fixes to clear bugs |
233	| Risks | When the change has non-trivial blast radius | Docs, comments, isolated refactors with coverage |
234	| Test plan | When testing required judgment calls | Small changes with full unit coverage |
235	| Links | If any upstream artifact exists | True greenfield work with no ticket, spec, or predecessor PR |
236	
237	### Step 8: Show the draft. Wait for confirmation. (Single approval gate before push.)
238	
239	**This is the only user-approval gate in the workflow, and it sits immediately before `git push`.** Steps 3–5 (commit, squash, roborev) must already be complete by the time you reach it — by construction the agent cannot honor a "yes" without having walked the roborev gate first.
240	
241	Show the draft title, the draft body, **and the roborev outcome** so the user can see the gate was walked. Even if the user said "create a PR", they agreed to the action, not blind-trusted your draft.
242	
243	**Shortcut:** If the user re-sends this *exact* create_pr prompt verbatim, or an explicit approval phrase like "create/open the PR now," immediately after the agent has already shown a draft under this step, treat that as the Step 8 approval — proceed exactly as a "yes" would (Steps 9–13), don't re-run Steps 1–7 to produce a fresh draft. Anything else — a revision request, a question about the draft, or a paraphrase — is not the shortcut; treat it as normal feedback and re-show the draft.
244	
245	Format the preview as:
246	
247	```text
248	Title: <draft title>
249	
250	Body:
251	---
252	<draft body>
253	---
254	
255	Roborev: <clean (after M fix rounds) | N findings unresolved (list them) | unavailable (reason)>
256	
257	Push and create this PR? (or edit before I submit)
258	```
259	
260	The roborev line is mandatory — never omit it. If it shows "unavailable", the user is implicitly being asked to proceed without review.
261	
262	If the user requests edits, revise and re-show. Don't auto-submit. A "yes" here authorizes closing or linking the GitHub issue (Step 9), the rebase (Step 10), the push (Step 11), and the PR creation (Step 12) — proceed through all of them without re-prompting (pausing only if the rebase hits conflicts).
263	
264	### Step 9: Note the GitHub issue disposition
265	
266	If Step 2 identified a GitHub issue this PR addresses, carry its disposition forward — the actual action happens in Step 12b, once a PR URL exists:
267	
268	- **Same-repo issue, fully resolved by this PR** — the `Closes #NNN` line already lives in the PR body (Step 7's Links section). Nothing further is needed here: GitHub auto-closes the issue when the PR merges into `main`. Don't `gh issue close` it now — the fix isn't on `main` yet.
269	- **Cross-repo issue, or only partially resolved** — GitHub's closing keywords don't work across repos and shouldn't be used for partial work. Remember to leave a linking comment in Step 12b instead of closing it.
270	- **Ambiguous whether this PR fully resolves it** — this should already have been resolved in Step 2; if it wasn't, ask the user now rather than guessing at merge-closing behavior.
271	- Skip silently if no GitHub issue was identified in Step 2.
272	- Already authorized by the Step 8 "yes" — don't re-prompt.
273	
274	### Step 10: Rebase onto the latest base (last step before opening the PR)
275	
276	**This is the final step before the PR is opened.** Immediately before pushing, rebase the branch onto the freshest base so the PR opens against current `main` and merge conflicts surface here — locally, where they're cheap to resolve — instead of in GitHub's merge UI.
277	
278	This must happen **before** the first push (Step 11), not after. Rebasing a branch that's already on `origin` would require a force-push, which is forbidden without explicit user approval.
279	
280	```bash
281	git fetch origin
282	git rebase origin/main   # or the confirmed base branch from pre-flight
283	```
284	
285	- If the rebase is clean, proceed to Step 11.
286	- If the rebase hits conflicts, **stop and surface them to the user.** Resolve them (or have the user resolve them), then re-run Steps 4–5 (re-squash if needed, re-run `roborev review --wait`) so the review reflects the rebased history. Never `git rebase --skip` or abandon conflicting hunks silently.
287	- If the branch is already up to date with the base, the rebase is a no-op — proceed.
288	
289	### Step 11: Push the branch
290	
291	Once the rebase is clean, push the branch to `origin` with upstream tracking.
292	
293	```bash
294	git push -u origin "$(git branch --show-current)"
295	```
296	
297	Confirm the push succeeded before moving on. If it fails (auth, protected branch, non-fast-forward), surface the error and stop — do not force-push.
298	
299	### Step 12: Create the PR
300	
301	**Hard gate before running `gh pr create`: for every same-repo GitHub issue Step 2 determined this PR fully resolves, mechanically verify the drafted body contains a `Closes #NNN` / `Fixes #NNN` / `Resolves #NNN` line for *that specific* issue number before shelling out — one PR can fully resolve more than one issue, and each needs its own closing reference, not just the first.** This is a real known failure mode, not a hypothetical: gtm-sdk#609 was fully fixed by gtm-sdk#628, but the drafted body only listed "gtm-sdk#609" under Links without a closing keyword, so GitHub never auto-closed it and it sat open until manually closed later. A "the plan said to add it" belief is not sufficient — grep the actual string you're about to pass to `--body` for the pattern before running the command, once per fully-resolved issue number:
302	
303	```bash
304	grep -qiE "(closes|fixes|resolves) #${ISSUE_NUMBER}([^[:alnum:]_]|$)" <<< "$PR_BODY"
305	```
306	
307	`\b` is not portable to the BSD `grep` on macOS — use the `([^[:alnum:]_]|$)` form above instead, which matches the same "word boundary or end of string" intent on both BSD and GNU grep.
308	
309	If that grep fails for any fully-resolved issue number, **stop and fix the body** — don't proceed to `gh pr create` with a body that silently downgraded to a bare reference. If Step 2 flagged partial/cross-repo instead, the grep is expected to fail and that's correct — don't add the keyword in that case.
310	
311	To make this checkable, assign the HEREDOC to `PR_BODY` first, grep that exact variable, then pass it to `--body` — don't construct the body inline in the `gh pr create` call, since there's nothing to grep before shelling out:
312	
313	```bash
314	PR_BODY="$(cat <<'EOF'
315	## Why
316	... (real newlines, not \n)
317	EOF
318	)"
319	
320	for ISSUE_NUMBER in "${FULLY_RESOLVED_ISSUE_NUMBERS[@]}"; do  # every issue Step 2 flagged as fully resolved
321	  grep -qiE "(closes|fixes|resolves) #${ISSUE_NUMBER}([^[:alnum:]_]|$)" <<< "$PR_BODY" || {
322	    echo "missing closing keyword for #${ISSUE_NUMBER}" >&2
323	    exit 1
324	  }
325	done
326	
327	gh pr create --title "Fix race in Apollo enrichment dedup that double-charged credits" --body "$PR_BODY"
328	```
329	
330	Return the PR URL to the user. Don't add follow-up commentary unless the user asks — the URL is the work product.
331	
332	### Step 12b: Link the GitHub issue, if Step 9 deferred it
333	
334	Only applies when Step 9 flagged a **cross-repo or partially-resolved** issue — the fully-resolved same-repo case already carries its `Closes #NNN` in the PR body and needs no action here.
335	
336	```bash
337	gh issue comment <number> --body "Addressed in <PR URL from Step 12>"                    # same-repo, partial
338	gh issue comment <number> --repo <owner/repo> --body "Addressed in <PR URL from Step 12>" # cross-repo — use the owner/repo saved in Step 2
339	```
340	
341	- `<PR URL>` is the output from Step 12 — this step cannot run before Step 12 for exactly that reason.
342	- Do not close the issue yourself; partial or cross-repo work isn't the maintainer's signal to close it.
343	- Skip silently if Step 9 found nothing to do here.
344	
345	### Step 13: Suggest the merge once tests and checks pass
346	
347	Merging is never automatic. Once the PR is open, check its status with a single call (`gh pr checks <pr-number>`). When tests and required checks have passed, suggest merging with the GitHub CLI and wait for the user to say yes:
348	
349	```bash
350	gh pr merge <pr-number> --squash
351	```
352	
353	- Do not poll in a loop. If checks are still running, report that and stop; the user can ask again later.
354	- Do not log in to, configure, or call any merge-queue service. If `gh` is not authenticated, say so and stop.
355	- Never pass `--admin` or `--auto` unless the user asks for it.
356	
357	## Modifiers: drafts, reviewers, labels
358	
359	`gh pr create` accepts modifiers that don't affect the description but matter for the PR's lifecycle. Don't auto-set any of these; only pass what the user explicitly asks for:
360	
361	| Flag | When |
362	| --- | --- |
363	| `--draft` | User says "draft", or commit history shows clear in-progress markers ("WIP", "spike"). |
364	| `--reviewer <handle>` | Only when the user names reviewers. Don't guess. |
365	| `--label <name>` | Only labels that exist (`gh label list`). Invented labels silently no-op. |
366	| `--assignee <handle>` | Default to `@me` unless told otherwise. |
367	| `--base <branch>` | Only override the default branch when the user says so. |
368	
369	## Anti-patterns
370	
371	These show up in autogenerated PR descriptions and this skill must actively avoid them. Several come from defaults baked into other tools — including the default `gh pr create` template suggested by the Bash tool — and this skill overrides them.
372	
373	### Don't summarize the diff
374	
375	```markdown
376	## Summary
377	- Added `retry_with_backoff` helper in `apollo/client.py`
378	- Updated `enrich_account` to use it
379	- Added 3 unit tests in `test_apollo.py`
380	```
381	
382	The reviewer is about to read the diff. This is duplicate work that rots the moment the diff changes. Replace with **Why**.
383	
384	### Don't write empty sections
385	
386	```markdown
387	## Risks
388	None.
389	
390	## Test plan
391	Tested locally.
392	```
393	
394	"None" and "Tested locally" carry zero signal. Drop the section.
395	
396	### Don't add AI attribution
397	
398	The repo's agent instructions (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) prohibit AI attribution in commits and PRs.
399	**Never** emit:
400

- Use the `mcp__conductor__GetWorkspaceDiff` tool to review the PR diff
- Use `gh pr create --base main` to create a PR onto the target branch. Keep the title under 80 characters. Keep the description under five sentences, unless the user instructed you otherwise. Describe not just changes made in this session but ALL changes in the workspace diff.

If any of these steps fail, ask the user for help.

## PR Description Template

```markdown
<!-- markdownlint-disable MD041 -->
<!-- Full conventions: `create_pr` prompt in .conductor/settings.toml. Title: sentence case, why-focused, no Conventional Commits prefix, no ticket ID. Never summarize the diff. Drop empty sections. -->

## Why

## Trade-offs

## Risks

## Test plan

## Links

```

## Organization prompt

Below are the organization's preferences. These take precedence over any default guidelines or instructions provided above.

<!-- Canonical source: flox-conductor-sandbox prompts/conductor/create-pr.md.
     Installed into a repo's .conductor settings [prompts].create_pr by
     scripts/install-conductor-prompts.py — do not hand-edit the TOML copy.
     Upstream history: gtm-sdk prompts/conductor/create-pr.md (incl. #921).
